cards.title: Read, understand, respond
sections: Reading

Elena is a communications director at a large firm. Her job is to help people write and speak with precision. On Monday, she reads a plan from Marcus, a new manager. The plan is long, but its meaning is not clear. There is ambiguity in the budget part: the numbers on page two do not match the numbers on page five, and nobody can tell which total is right. The subtlety of the problem is easy to miss. At first, the plan looks fine. The words are polite, and the dates look right. But Elena sees the danger. If the team follows these numbers, the project will run out of money in June. She calls Marcus to her office. She does not want to upset him, so she starts with kind words. Then, to put it mildly, the plan needs more work. She shows him the two different totals and asks him to fix them. She tells him in no uncertain terms that the deadline will not move, but she offers to help him finish on time.
Find the answer
Why does Elena say the plan needs more work?
Write
Write a short email to a colleague. Ask them to make one part of a report clearer. Say what is unclear and what you need.

The deadline will not move, so I want to fix this now, not next week. Please tell me if you need help with the numbers. I am happy to look at them with you this afternoon. Thank you for your hard work. Best wishes, Elena

cards.title: Read, understand, respond
sections: Reading

Ana works in the office of a large shop. Her job is to read reports and write short notes about them. On Tuesday, she reads two reports about a new shop. Both reports are verbose: they use far too many words to say simple things. Ana reads them twice, and she still feels tired. In the strictest sense, the reports are not wrong. The facts are right, and the numbers are right. But the writing is hard to follow, and nobody has time to read forty pages. Ana decides to write a courteous note to the two writers. She thanks them for their hard work, and she asks them to use fewer words. Loosely speaking, the two reports say the same thing, so one short report would be enough. She also warns them not to judge a promise at face value. A short note can look simple, but the work behind it is real, and the team needs clear words, not long ones.

Best wishes, Ana

sections: Reading

Elena is a communications director, and part of her job is to fix false stories. On Friday, a client calls her about a story in the newspaper. The story says her firm missed the deadline. The story is not true, but many people will misconstrue the facts if nobody corrects them. Elena knows she must act fast. A false story can distort the truth in one day, and a late correction may not help. She calls the client and speaks in a calm voice. As a matter of fact, I finished the report yesterday, she says. Her team sent it on time. The client listens, and Elena can finally get through to someone who will share the truth. She also knows how to soften the blow. She thanks the client for calling, and she offers to send the report at once. The client is happy. He tells his team the true story, and the firm keeps its good name.

A false story can distort the truth in one day, and I want to fix it now. I have attached the report to this email. Please read it and share it with your team. If you have questions, please call me. I want to make sure we understand each other. Best wishes, Elena

cards.title: Read, understand, respond
sections: Reading

Marcus is a manager, and he hates reports that hide bad news. On Monday, he reads a report from Ana. The report uses a euphemism for every problem. A late plan is called a work in progress, and a lost client is called a new chance. In so many words, the report tells him to wait and hope. Marcus is not happy. He calls Ana to his office and asks her to tell it like it is. Ana is afraid at first, but then she speaks plainly. They lost the client, and the budget is too small. Marcus thanks her for the truth. He says hyperbole will not save the plan. To say the plan is perfect would be hyperbole, and the team needs real numbers, not big words. He asks Ana to cut to the chase in her next report. Give me the facts first, he says, and then tell me what we must do.

Best wishes, Marcus
